title: Government spending multipliers
text: Ramey and Zubairy (2018, JPE) estimate how much GDP rises when government spending rises, using more than a century of US quarterly data. This page replicates the baseline linear model from their Stata program jordagk.do: the impulse responses, the one-step cumulative multiplier, the two-step multiplier and the weak-instrument diagnostic. The authors build every lead, cumulated sum and lag by hand and loop ivreg2 over horizons. Here each is a single call.

title: Government spending multipliers
text:
Data and specification
The cleaned dataset ships with the package as docs/src/data/ramey_zubairy.csv, built from the replication package with the variable definitions of jordagk.do. GDP and spending are divided by potential GDP (the Gordon–Krenn normalization), so regression coefficients are already in dollars of GDP per dollar of spending.

title: Government spending multipliers
text:
Impulse responses
The responses of spending and GDP at horizon \(h\) are the coefficients on the shock in \(x_{t+h} = \alpha_h + \beta_h s_t + \gamma_h' w_{t-1} + u_{t+h}\). leads(x) puts \(x_{t+h}\) on the left and lp runs the regression for every \(h\) up to horizon:

irf_y_news = lp(@formula(leads(y) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)),
    rz; horizon = 20)
irf_g_news = lp(@formula(leads(g) ~ newsy + lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)),
    rz; horizon = 20)
irf_y_bp = lp(@formula(leads(y) ~ bp + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), rz; horizon = 20)
irf_g_bp = lp(@formula(leads(g) ~ bp + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), rz; horizon = 20)

hac = Bartlett{NeweyWest}()      # Newey–West, automatic bandwidth
summarize(irf_y_news, hac; term = :newsy, level = 0.90)

After a news shock both responses are hump-shaped: spending peaks at 0.37 after 11 quarters, GDP at 0.29 after 10. Under Blanchard–Perotti the shock is current spending, so spending moves one for one on impact, keeps rising to 2.25 after 3 quarters, then declines.

title: Government spending multipliers
text:
The one-step cumulative multiplier
The multiplier at horizon \(h\) is cumulative extra GDP per cumulative extra dollar of spending. Ramey and Zubairy estimate it in one step, as \(m_h\) in
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{h} y_{t+j} = \alpha_h + m_h \sum_{j=0}^{h} g_{t+j} + \gamma_h' w_{t-1} + u_{t+h},
\]
with cumulative spending instrumented by the shock \(s_t\). Both sides move with the horizon, and cumul handles either side, so lpiv returns the whole multiplier path at once:

mult_news = lpiv(TSLS(), @formula(cumul(y) ~ (cumul(g) ~ newsy) +
                                  lags(newsy, 4) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)), rz; horizon = 20)
mult_bp = lpiv(TSLS(), @formula(cumul(y) ~ (cumul(g) ~ bp) + lags(y, 4) + lags(g, 4)),
    rz; horizon = 20)

s_news = summarize(mult_news, hac; level = 0.90)   # the multiplier is `shock`, no `term`
s_bp = summarize(mult_bp, hac; level = 0.90)
nobs(mult_bp)[[1, 9, 21]]                          # h = 0, 8, 20: Stata's samples

At these 13 horizons, for both shocks, every point estimate is within 0.19 published standard errors of the authors’ value, with a median gap of 0.03. The remaining difference is most likely the data vintage: the spreadsheet of published numbers predates the last revision of the shipped data by a week.
The standard errors differ more, 0.77 to 1.14 times the published ones, for two reasons:

Bandwidth. The paper uses ivreg2, robust bw(auto). Both sides implement the Newey–West (1994) automatic rule, but they select different bandwidths on the same regression. With a fixed bandwidth, Bartlett(b) here and bw(b) in Stata, coefficients and IV standard errors agree to about \(10^{-10}\).
Degrees of freedom. ivreg2 applies no small-sample factor. The standard errors here, IV and OLS alike, carry \(n/(n-k)\) and are 1–3% larger than Stata’s ivreg2 equivalents.

title: Government spending multipliers
text:
The two-step multiplier
The paper’s alternative estimator is the ratio of the cumulative sums of the two impulse responses, \(\sum_{j \le h} \hat\beta^y_j \,/\, \sum_{j \le h} \hat\beta^g_j\):

twostep(ry, rg, shock) = cumsum(coefpath(ry; term = shock)) ./
                         cumsum(coefpath(rg; term = shock))
two_news = twostep(irf_y_news, irf_g_news, :newsy)
two_bp = twostep(irf_y_bp, irf_g_bp, :bp)
(news = maximum(abs.(two_news .- s_news.coef)), bp = maximum(abs.(two_bp .- s_bp.coef)))

(news = 0.0031353020818054578, bp = 0.0003613935999802753)


The two estimators agree to within 0.0031 (news) and 0.0004 (Blanchard–Perotti) at every horizon, because here the one-step regressions use the same sample as the impulse-response regressions. Ramey and Zubairy note that the two can diverge in other specifications, precisely when the samples differ.

title: Government spending multipliers
text:
Is the instrument strong enough?
A multiplier estimated with a weak instrument is biased and its bands undercover. weakivtest computes the Montiel Olea–Pflueger effective F at each horizon, from the HAC covariance attached to the model:

w_news = weakivtest(mult_news + vcov(hac))         # one test per horizon
w_bp = weakivtest(mult_bp + vcov(hac))
w_news[9]                                          # two years out


Montiel-Pflueger robust weak instrument test

TSLS coefficient (SE):          0.6690 (  0.0625)
LIML coefficient (SE):          0.6690 (  0.0625)
GMMf coefficient (SE):          0.6690 (  0.0625)
kappa:                              1.0000
F[nonrobust]:                       71.863
F[effective]:                       18.087
F[robust]:                          18.087
Confidence level alpha:               5%
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Use:
  Compare F[effective] or F[robust] to the common critical values below.
  If F exceeds the critical value at tau, weak-IV bias is below that tau bound.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
tau              Common
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
tau=5%           37.418
tau=10%          23.109
tau=20%          15.062
tau=30%          12.045
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────





Montiel Olea–Pflueger effective F, log scale. The dashed line is the 5% critical value for a worst-case bias of 10%.


The news instrument never clears the critical value of 23.11: its effective F peaks at 19.57 at 5 quarters. Blanchard–Perotti is strong at short horizons and falls below the threshold from horizon 11 on. At \(h = 0\) its instrument is the regressor: the regression treats it as exogenous, there is no first stage to test (weakivtest returns nothing), and the figure omits that point. Ramey and Zubairy respond to weak instruments with Anderson–Rubin inference, which the package does not implement yet.

title: LocalProjections.jl
text: These pages work through the package’s examples in full. Every number, table and figure is computed from the package when the site is rendered, so the text cannot drift from the code.

title: LocalProjections.jl
text:
Install
using Pkg
Pkg.add(url = "https://github.com/andrerecio/LocalProjections.jl")
Julia 1.13 or newer is required. Two dependencies, Regress.jl and MacroEconometricTools.jl, are unregistered and are resolved from GitHub automatically.
This is a fork of Giuseppe Ragusa’s LocalProjections.jl, version 0.2. It adds HAR inference with equal-weighted-cosine (EWC) variances and Student-\(t\) critical values, the Herbst–Johannsen bias correction, the VAR moving-block bootstrap, VAR lag selection, state-dependent projections, long-difference projections, the Hall–Barro–Redlick transformation for fiscal multipliers, Gorodnichenko–Lee variance decompositions, and joint inference across horizons with sup-t simultaneous bands.

title: LocalProjections.jl
section: The workflow in a few lines
text:
The workflow in a few lines
using LocalProjections, StatsModels, CovarianceMatrices, Plots
r = lp(@formula(leads(y) ~ shock + lags(y, 4) + lags(shock, 4)), df; horizon = 20)
summarize(r, Bartlett{NeweyWest}(); level = 0.90)   # path, s.e. and bands
plot(r, EWC(ewc_bandwidth(r)); term = :shock, levels = [0.68, 0.90])
The left-hand side sets the response: leads(y) for \(y_{t+h}\), cumul(y) for \(\sum_{j \le h} y_{t+j}\), anchor(y, z) for \(y_{t+h} - z_t\), ldiff(y) for \(y_{t+h} - y_{t-1}\), hbr(x, y) for \((x_{t+h} - x_{t-1}) / y_{t-1}\). lpiv(TSLS(), ...) takes an instrumented regressor, (cumul(g) ~ z), and the covariance estimator is any estimator from CovarianceMatrices.jl.

title: LocalProjections.jl
text:
Rebuilding these pages
From docs/quarto/:
julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
quarto render
Computed results are frozen in _freeze/, so a page is re-run only when its source changes. A change to the package itself does not invalidate them: re-render a page explicitly (quarto render ramey-zubairy.qmd always executes) or delete _freeze/. This build: LocalProjections at commit c5b7d3c, Julia 1.13.1.

title: Variance decompositions and joint inference
text: Mikkel Plagborg-Møller’s short course Local projections for applied macroeconomics (2026) works one example through its Stata code: the effect of global temperature shocks on world GDP, after Bilal and Känzig (2026). This page reruns two of its steps that the package did not have: the variance decomposition of lecture 1, which asks how much of the GDP forecast error the temperature shock explains, and the joint inference of lecture 3, a Wald test of all horizons at once and a simultaneous confidence band. In Stata they take a loop of regress/predict, suest and a user-written command; here they are implicitfevd, jointtest and bands = :supt. Every number is checked against the course’s Stata commands at the end of the page.

title: Variance decompositions and joint inference
text:
Data and specification
The course’s extract of the Bilal–Känzig data ships as docs/src/data/bilal_kanzig.csv: annual, 1960–2019, with world real GDP per capita (100·log, lnrgdppc_world_pwt), the global temperature anomaly (gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s, the Hamilton-filter forecast error of global temperature in °C), a global-recession indicator, the log oil price and the one-year Treasury yield.

bk = bk_data()
first(bk[:, [:year, :lnrgdppc_world_pwt, :gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s, :recessiondates]], 3)

With \(y_t\) log GDP, \(x_t\) the anomaly, \(r_t\) the recession indicator and \(w_t\) the four lagged series, the local projection is
\[
y_{t+h} = \mu_h + \theta_h x_t + \sum_{j=0}^{2} \gamma_{h,j} r_{t-j}
        + \sum_{j=1}^{2} \delta_{h,j}' w_{t-j} + \xi_{h,t+h}, \qquad h = 0, \dots, 10,
\]
with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, the course’s reg ..., robust. The lagged controls make them valid without a HAC correction (lag augmentation).

m = lp(@formula(leads(lnrgdppc_world_pwt) ~ gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s + recessiondates +
                lags(recessiondates, 2) + lags(lnrgdppc_world_pwt, 2) +
                lags(gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s, 2) + lags(lnpoil_wti, 2) + lags(treasury1y, 2)),
       bk; horizon = 10)
summarize(m; level = 0.68)

title: Variance decompositions and joint inference
text:
The implicit shock
By Frisch–Waugh, \(\theta_h\) is the response to \(\tilde x_t\), the residual of \(x_t\) on all the controls: the movement in temperature that recessions and past economic conditions do not explain. implicitshock returns it, aligned with the rows of the data:

x̃ = implicitshock(m)
std(filter(isfinite, x̃))

0.10029931207558151





The implicit temperature shock (°C), the residual of the anomaly on the controls.


Its standard deviation, 0.10 °C, is the size of a typical shock, so a 1 °C impulse is about 10 standard deviations, an unusually large one.

title: Variance decompositions and joint inference
text:
Variance decomposition
How much of the uncertainty about future GDP is due to temperature shocks? The course’s recipe, a version of Gorodnichenko and Lee (2020), runs at each horizon two regressions:

regress \(y_{t+h}\) on the controls (everything but \(x_t\)) and keep the forecast error \(\hat f_{h,t+h}\);
regress \(\hat f_{h,t+h}\) on a constant and \(\tilde x_t, \tilde x_{t+1}, \dots,
\tilde x_{t+h}\); the share is its \(R^2\).

The share is the fraction of the forecast-error variance that would disappear if the current and future shocks were known. implicitfevd runs both steps from the fitted projection:

fv = implicitfevd(m)


ImplicitFEVD (R² of the forecast error on the implicit shock)
  Response:   lnrgdppc_world_pwt
  Shock:      gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s (residual on the controls, 58 rows)
  Formula:    :(leads(lnrgdppc_world_pwt)) ~ gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s + recessiondates + :(lags(recessiondates, 2)) + :(lags(lnrgdppc_world_pwt, 2)) + :(lags(gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s, 2)) + :(lags(lnpoil_wti, 2)) + :(lags(treasury1y, 2))

Share of the forecast-error variance of world GDP due to temperature shocks.


Temperature shocks explain 8.5% of the variance of the two-year GDP forecast error and 49.2% of the seven-year one, the figures on the course’s slides.
The package’s fevd, the port of Gorodnichenko and Lee’s own code, would not accept this specification as it stands: it treats the shock as observed and demeaned rather than residualized, conditions only on lagged variables, and needs a cumul or ldiff response. implicitfevd follows the course instead: the shock is \(\tilde x_t\), the forecast error conditions on the contemporaneous recession indicator too, and the \(R^2\) is the centred one of a regression with a constant. It has no standard errors, as in the course.

title: Variance decompositions and joint inference
text:
Joint inference across horizons
The 68% band above covers each horizon with probability 0.68 separately. A hypothesis about several horizons needs the covariance of the estimates across horizons, which are correlated because the regressions share their observations. jointvcov stacks the scores of every horizon on one time axis (Stata’s suest), and jointtest is the Wald test that the response is zero at every horizon:

t = jointtest(m)

Joint Wald test across horizons
  Term:       gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s
  H₀:         θ_h = 0 for h ∈ {0:10}
  Vcov:       CovarianceMatrices.HR1()
  chi2(11) = 23.1552
  p-value:    0.0168


The estimates are strongly correlated across neighbouring horizons (the correlation of \(\hat\theta_5\) and \(\hat\theta_6\) is 0.85), so the pointwise band cannot be read as a joint statement. The null of no effect at any horizon is rejected with a p-value of 0.017.
A simultaneous band covers the whole response with probability 0.68. The sup-t band of Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2019) widens the pointwise band by a common critical value, the 68% quantile of \(\max_h |\hat\theta_h - \theta_h| /
\mathrm{se}_h\), simulated from that correlation:

c68 = supt_critical_value(m; level = 0.68)

1.8771803288591733





Response of world GDP per capita (%) to a 1 °C temperature shock: 68% pointwise band (shaded) and 68% sup-t simultaneous band (dashed).


The simultaneous band uses 1.88 standard errors instead of one. It still excludes zero at horizons 4–8, so the negative effect of temperature shocks on GDP survives the joint reading. At the 90% level (critical value 2.42) it excludes zero at horizons 5–6. Any shape restriction can be checked the same way: a monotone response, for instance, is rejected if no monotone function fits inside the band.
bands = :supt works in summarize, plot and irfplot alike:
summarize(m; level = 0.68, bands = :supt)
plot(m; levels = [0.68], bands = :supt)
With an EWC(B) estimator the test becomes the fixed-smoothing \(F_{m,\,B-m+1}\) test and the sup-t draws come from the fixed-\(b\) limit, whose margins are Student-\(t_B\). With \(T = 58\) the LLSW rule gives only 6 cosine terms, fewer than the eleven horizons, and an EWC variance has rank at most \(B\), so the joint test is available only for a few horizons at a time:

jointtest(m, EWC(ewc_bandwidth(m)); horizons = 4:8)

Joint Wald test across horizons
  Term:       gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s
  H₀:         θ_h = 0 for h ∈ {4:8}
  Vcov:       CovarianceMatrices.EWC(6)
  F(5, 2) = 1.186   (Wald = 17.7899, fixed-b EWC)
  p-value:    0.5164

0.0168



The covariance matrix itself matches suest to about \(10^{-10}\) of its scale. The design is ill-conditioned (log GDP near 900 next to its own lags), so the smallest entries agree to fewer digits.
The sup-t critical value depends only on the correlation, which every heteroskedasticity-robust estimator shares, so it does not depend on the convention. The course computes it with Kessler’s estimate_supt_critical_value, by default from 1000 drawnorm draws (seed 192837), which gives 1.8907 at 68%. Applied to those same draws, the package’s quantile rule returns the same number to the last digit. Stata’s draws cannot be reproduced in Julia, so the default supt_critical_value (100,000 draws of its own) is compared with a million Stata draws:

title: Levels or long differences?
text: Piger and Stockwell (2025, Journal of Applied Econometrics) ask whether a local projection with an observed shock should be estimated with the response in levels, \(y_{t+h}\), or in long differences, \(y_{t+h} - y_{t-1}\). This page reruns the application of their paper (Figure 20): the responses of US industrial production and consumer prices to the Jarocinski–Karadi (2020) monetary-policy and central-bank-information shocks, estimated both ways. In their MATLAB code each specification is a hand-built loop over horizons. Here each is one lp call.

title: Levels or long differences?
text:
Data and specification
The monthly dataset from their replication package ships with the package as docs/src/data/piger_stockwell.csv: the two shocks (mp, cbi) and five series, 100·log industrial production (lip), CPI (lcpi) and S&P 500 (lsp500), the excess bond premium (ebp) and the one-year Treasury yield (gs1). As in their code, the sample ends in 2019:12 and each shock is divided by its standard deviation.

The shocks begin in 1990:2 and are missing before. Those months are not estimation rows, but the lagged controls of the first estimation rows reach back into them: lp builds lags and leads on the full time axis and only then drops the incomplete rows of each horizon.
For a response \(y\) and shock \(s_t\), with \(x_t\) the five series, the two specifications are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{levels:}\quad & y_{t+h} = \alpha_h + \beta_h s_t + \sum_{j=1}^{12} \gamma_{h,j}' x_{t-j} + u_{t+h}, \\
\text{long differences:}\quad & y_{t+h} - y_{t-1} = \alpha_h + \beta_h s_t + \sum_{j=1}^{12} \gamma_{h,j}' \Delta x_{t-j} + u_{t+h}.
\end{aligned}
\]
ldiff(y) builds the long difference and lags(firstdiff(x), 12) the lagged first differences:

levels = lp(@formula(leads(lip) ~ mp + lags(lip, 12) + lags(lcpi, 12) +
                     lags(lsp500, 12) + lags(ebp, 12) + lags(gs1, 12)), ps; horizon = 36)
diffs = lp(@formula(ldiff(lip) ~ mp + lags(firstdiff(lip), 12) + lags(firstdiff(lcpi), 12) +
                    lags(firstdiff(lsp500), 12) + lags(firstdiff(ebp), 12) +
                    lags(firstdiff(gs1), 12)), ps; horizon = 36)

nw = Bartlett(38)       # Newey–West with 37 lags (h_max + 1), as in their code
summarize(diffs, nw; level = 0.90)

Standard errors follow their code: Newey–West with 37 lags at every horizon and the \(n/(n-k)\) small-sample factor. Bartlett(38) is that estimator, since a Bartlett bandwidth of \(b\) weights lags \(1, \dots, b-1\).

title: Levels or long differences?
text:
Impulse responses



Responses to a one-standard-deviation shock. Solid navy: long differences; dashed brick: levels. 90% bands, Newey–West with 37 lags.



Three years after a monetary-policy shock, industrial production is -0.33 in long differences and 0.09 in levels.

The two specifications agree over the first months and then part. In levels the responses drift back toward zero at long horizons; in long differences they stay persistent. The price is precision: at 36 months the long-difference standard errors are 1.58 to 2.15 times the levels ones across the four panels. This is the trade-off the paper studies. In its simulations, levels projections on persistent data are biased toward zero at long horizons, and long differences remove much of that bias at the cost of a larger variance.

title: Levels or long differences?
text:
Checks
The long-difference response is an anchored response, \(y_{t+h}\) minus a baseline fixed at \(t\), with the baseline \(y_{t-1}\). Written with anchor, the same regression gives the same path:

anchored = lp(@formula(anchor(lip, lag(lip)) ~ mp + lags(firstdiff(lip), 12) +
                       lags(firstdiff(lcpi), 12) + lags(firstdiff(lsp500), 12) +
                       lags(firstdiff(ebp), 12) + lags(firstdiff(gs1), 12)), ps;
    horizon = 36)
maximum(abs.(coefpath(anchored) .- coefpath(diffs)))

0.0


And the regression at any single horizon is ordinary least squares on columns built by hand, the way their MATLAB loop builds them:

h = 24
T = nrow(ps)
rows = 14:(T - h)                                   # 1990:2 to T − h
Δ(v) = [NaN; diff(Float64.(v))]
X = hcat(Float64.(ps.mp[rows]), ones(length(rows)),
    [Δ(ps[!, v])[rows .- j] for v in (:lip, :lcpi, :lsp500, :ebp, :gs1), j in 1:12]...)
Y = ps.lip[rows .+ h] .- ps.lip[rows .- 1]
(by_hand = (X \ Y)[1], ldiff = coefpath(diffs)[h + 1])

(by_hand = -0.27233853739248953, ldiff = -0.27233853739248887)


Beyond this page, the paths were checked against Stata (newey, lag(37) on variables built with time-series operators) and against a line-by-line port of the authors’ MATLAB loop, including its Newey–West sum. The long-difference coefficients and standard errors agree with both to \(10^{-14}\) at every horizon, on identical samples; the levels ones to \(10^{-6}\), the precision allowed by 61 nearly collinear log-level regressors.

title: Levels or long differences?
text:
Other long-difference responses
ldiff has two relatives. cumul(ldiff(y)) sums the long differences over horizons \(0, \dots, h\), for cumulative responses. hbr(x, y) divides the change by a lagged scale variable, \((x_{t+h} - x_{t-1}) / y_{t-1}\): the Hall–Barro–Redlick transformation used for fiscal multipliers, where output and spending changes are both measured as shares of lagged GDP. All of them can also appear on the right-hand side, as the instrumented regressor of a cumulative multiplier:
lpiv(TSLS(), @formula(cumul(hbr(gdp)) ~ (cumul(hbr(gov, gdp)) ~ news) +
              lags(news, 4) + lags(log(gdp), 4) + lags(log(gov), 4)), df; horizon = 20)
